Differentiable Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning

Sitao Cheng*, Tianle Li*, Xuhan Huang*, Xunjian Yin, Difan Zou

Paper ↗Code ↗

DERL learns how to combine simple reward signals: a meta-optimizer proposes rewards, trains a policy with them, and improves from that policy's validation performance.

01 / The research question

More reward signals can teach the wrong behavior

A final correct-or-incorrect reward is clear but sparse. Adding checks for formatting, intermediate progress, or explicit reasoning steps creates more feedback, yet it also changes what the policy is encouraged to do. The design problem is not only obtaining these signals; it is deciding how they should interact.

The mathematical reasoning comparison makes this tension concrete. With combined GSM8K and MATH training data, adding a format reward improves GSM8K from 82.6% to 86.4%, while MATH falls from 58.8% to 55.9%. A seemingly helpful auxiliary criterion can favor one evaluation setting at another’s expense. A fixed average of available signals has a similar trade-off.

02 / Inside the method

Judge a reward by the policy it teaches

DERL turns reward design into the action space of a second trainable model. This meta-optimizer proposes a symbolic expression over supplied atomic checks. An inner policy is trained with that expression; its held-out task performance then becomes the outer reward. GRPO updates both levels, but for different objectives: the policy optimizes the generated reward, while the generator optimizes the policy’s subsequent validation performance.

A concrete example from the agent setup uses six step rewards: [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0]. Averaging the first, middle, and final thirds gives three primitives, 0.5, 1, and 0, alongside the final success signal. Their combination matters: multiplying all three would erase the early progress because the final segment is zero; averaging would preserve some credit. These are explanatory alternatives, not a claim that either is the learned optimum.

Standard DERL restarts the inner policy from the base model for each candidate reward, helping attribute validation differences to reward design. DERL-pop instead continues from the best policy of the previous round, allowing rewards to adapt as the learner changes. Valid-format SFT examples, constrained decoding, and penalties for invalid expressions keep reward proposals executable.

  1. 01

    Compose a reward

    A trainable meta-optimizer combines task-specific checks and arithmetic operations into a reward function.

  2. 02

    Train a policy

    Use the proposed reward to optimize an inner policy with GRPO.

  3. 03

    Learn from validation

    Held-out policy performance becomes the RL reward used to update the meta-optimizer.

03 / Reading the evidence

Generalization requires more than dense feedback

  • 65.0%

    ALFWorld · hardest split

    Standard DERL reaches 65.0% task success on L2, compared with 56.3% for RLVMR using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

  • 43.0%

    ScienceWorld · L1 split

    Standard DERL improves success over RLVMR's 34.4%, supporting reward learning beyond the household-task benchmark in the same evaluation.

On ALFWorld, averaging the primitives improves success on the familiar L0 split from 76.6% to 88.1%, but barely changes the held-out-task L2 split: 29.7% to 30.5%. Standard DERL reaches 65.0% on L2. The comparison supports learning the combination rather than assuming that denser feedback alone transfers. On combined-data mathematical training, its 87.0% GSM8K and 60.2% MATH results also avoid the simple format reward’s observed trade-off.

The outer update is a policy-gradient estimate over generated reward programs; it does not require differentiating through discrete task correctness or backpropagating through every inner training step. The cost is substantial repeated policy training. Available primitives still define the search space, and a reward generator cannot evaluate a useful property that its supplied checks never expose.

Research summary

The design of effective reward functions presents a central and often arduous challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly when developing autonomous agents for complex reasoning tasks. While automated reward optimization approaches exist, they typically rely on derivative-free evolutionary heuristics that treat the reward function as a black box, failing to capture the causal relationship between reward structure and task performance. To bridge this gap, we propose Differentiable Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (DERL), a bi-level framework that enables the autonomous discovery of optimal reward signals. In DERL, a Meta-Optimizer evolves a reward function (i.e., Meta-Reward) by composing structured atomic primitives, guiding the training of an inner-loop policy. Crucially, unlike previous evolution, DERL is differentiable in its meta-optimization: it treats the inner-loop validation performance as a signal to update the Meta-Optimizer via reinforcement learning. This allows DERL to approximate the "meta-gradient" of task success, progressively learning to generate denser and more actionable feedback. We validate DERL across three distinct domains: robotic agent (ALFWorld), scientific simulation (ScienceWorld), and mathematical reasoning (GSM8k, MATH). Experimental results show that DERL achieves state-of-the-art performance on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, significantly outperforming methods relying on heuristic rewards, especially in out-of-distribution scenarios. Analysis of the evolutionary trajectory demonstrates that DERL successfully captures the intrinsic structure of tasks, enabling self-improving agent alignment without human intervention.
